Cāpāla Chapter The Discourse on the Far Shore At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one who has crossed over and gone beyond, not for one who has not crossed over and has not gone beyond; it is for one who has reached the further shore and stands on firm ground, not for one who has not reached the further shore and stands on the near shore. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “But how, Bhante, is one ‘one who has crossed over and gone beyond,’ and how is one ‘one who has not crossed over and has not gone beyond’? How is one ‘one who has reached the further shore and stands on firm ground,’ and how is one ‘one who has not reached the further shore and stands on the near shore’? “Bhikkhu, one who possesses the aggregate of virtue that is untorn, unrent, unblotched, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped at, and conducive to concentration is called ‘one who has crossed over and gone beyond. One who does not possess the aggregate of virtue... is called ‘one who has not crossed over and has not gone beyond. One who possesses the aggregate of concentration that is untorn... and conducive to wisdom is called ‘one who has crossed over and gone beyond. One who does not possess the aggregate of concentration... is called ‘one who has not crossed over and has not gone beyond. One who possesses the aggregate of wisdom that is untorn... and leads to the complete destruction of suffering is called ‘one who has crossed over and gone beyond. One who does not possess the aggregate of wisdom... is called ‘one who has not crossed over and has not gone beyond. One who possesses the aggregate of liberation that is untorn... and is the fruit of the final knowledge is called ‘one who has crossed over and gone beyond. One who does not possess the aggregate of liberation... is called ‘one who has not crossed over and has not gone beyond. One who possesses the aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation that is untorn... and is the fruit of the final knowledge is called ‘one who has crossed over and gone beyond. One who does not possess the aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation... is called ‘one who has not crossed over and has not gone beyond. It is in this way, bhikkhu, that one is ‘one who has crossed over and gone beyond,’ and in this way one is ‘one who has not crossed over and has not gone beyond. It is in this way that one is ‘one who has reached the further shore and stands on firm ground,’ and in this way one is ‘one who has not reached the further shore and stands on the near shore. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, that bhikkhu delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one who has crossed over and gone beyond, not for one who has not crossed over and has not gone beyond; it is for one who has reached the further shore and stands on firm ground, not for one who has not reached the further shore and stands on the near shore. [As above, with the same questions and answers regarding the aggregates of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation. “This, bhikkhus, is called ‘the near shore,’ and this is called ‘the far shore. What, bhikkhus, is the near shore? It is the five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. This is called the near shore. And what, bhikkhus, is the far shore? It is the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion. This is called the far shore. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend,” they replied. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, the Blessed One has taught the near shore and the far shore. For us, friends, it is appropriate to go to the Blessed One and ask him about the meaning of this. As the Blessed One explains it to us, so we shall bear it in mind. “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported everything that had occurred, adding: “It would be good, Bhante, if the Blessed One would explain the meaning of this. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will bear it in mind. “Ānanda, the near shore is the five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging... and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These are the near shore. And what, Ānanda, is the far shore? It is the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion. This is the far shore. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having understood the meaning of the Blessed One’s words, addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, the Blessed One has taught the near shore and the far shore. The near shore is the five aggregates subject to clinging. The far shore is the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one who has crossed over and gone beyond, not for one who has not crossed over and has not gone beyond; it is for one who has reached the further shore and stands on firm ground, not for one who has not reached the further shore and stands on the near shore. [As above. “This, bhikkhus, is called ‘the near shore,’ and this is called ‘the far shore. What, bhikkhus, is the near shore? It is the six internal sense bases. What six? The eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, the tongue-base, the body-base, and the mind-base. This is called the near shore. And what, bhikkhus, is the far shore? It is the six external sense bases. What six? The form-base, the sound-base, the odor-base, the taste-base, the tangible-base, and the mental-phenomena-base. This is called the far shore. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then the Venerable Ānanda... [as above] ...addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, the Blessed One has taught the near shore and the far shore. The near shore is the six internal sense bases. The far shore is the six external sense bases. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one who has crossed over and gone beyond, not for one who has not crossed over and has not gone beyond; it is for one who has reached the further shore and stands on firm ground, not for one who has not reached the further shore and stands on the near shore. [As above. “This, bhikkhus, is called ‘the near shore,’ and this is called ‘the far shore. What, bhikkhus, is the near shore? It is ignorance. This is called the near shore. And what, bhikkhus, is the far shore? It is true knowledge. This is called the far shore. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then the Venerable Ānanda... [as above] ...addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, the Blessed One has taught the near shore and the far shore. The near shore is ignorance. The far shore is true knowledge. Thus have I heard. “Bhikkhus, these four bases for spiritual power, when developed and cultivated, lead to going from the near shore to the far shore.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the basis for spiritual power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving.”
He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of energy and volitional formations of striving;
he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of mind and volitional formations of striving;
he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of investigation and volitional formations of striving.
“Monks, these four bases for spiritual power, when developed and cultivated, lead to going from the near shore to the far shore.
Thus was the first [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 51.2 (SN 51.2, PTS SN v 254)
1. The Chapter on Cāpāla, Discourse on What is Missed:
“Bhikkhus, for whoever the four bases of psychic power have been missed, the Noble Path leading rightly to the destruction of suffering has been missed by them.”
“Bhikkhus, for whoever has undertaken the four bases for spiritual power, the noble path leading rightly to the destruction of suffering has been undertaken by them.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the basis for spiritual power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving.”

He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of energy and the volitional formations of striving; ...pe... he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of mind and the volitional formations of striving; ...pe... he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of investigation and the volitional formations of striving.
“Bhikkhus, for whoever has neglected these four bases for psychic power, the Noble Path leading rightly to the destruction of suffering has been neglected by them.
Bhikkhus, for whoever has undertaken these four bases for psychic power, the Noble Path leading rightly to the destruction of suffering has been undertaken by them.
The second [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 51.3 (SN 51.3, PTS SN v 255) 1. Cāpāla Vagga The Noble One Discourse (Ariyasutta) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these four noble lineages. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person is content with any kind of robe, any kind of almsfood, any kind of lodging, and any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick. He dwells possessing the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, flawless, unblemished, unblotched, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. He dwells possessing the four foundations of mindfulness. He develops the seven factors of enlightenment dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in relinquishment. This, bhikkhus, is the first noble lineage. “Again, bhikkhus, a certain person is not content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, or medicinal requisites for the sick; yet he dwells possessing the virtues dear to the noble ones... [as above] ...resulting in relinquishment. This, bhikkhus, is the second noble lineage. “Again, bhikkhus, a certain person is not content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, or medicinal requisites for the sick; nor does he dwell possessing the virtues dear to the noble ones... [as above] ...resulting in relinquishment. However, he is intent upon the higher Dhamma and the higher Discipline, and he dwells devoted to the detailed examination of those things that have been well-expounded by the Teacher. This, bhikkhus, is the third noble lineage. “Again, bhikkhus, a certain person is not content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, or medicinal requisites for the sick; nor does he dwell possessing the virtues dear to the noble ones... [as above] ...resulting in relinquishment; nor is he intent upon the higher Dhamma and the higher Discipline, devoted to the detailed examination of those things well-expounded by the Teacher. However, he gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth noble lineage. “These, bhikkhus, are the four noble lineages.”
“Bhikkhus, these four bases for spiritual power, when developed and cultivated, are noble and emancipating; they lead the one who practices them to the complete destruction of suffering.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the basis for spiritual power endowed with concentration of desire and volitional formations of striving.”

He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of energy and the volitional formations of striving; ... pe ... he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of mind and the volitional formations of striving; ... pe ... he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of investigation and the volitional formations of striving.
“Monks, these four bases for spiritual power, when developed and cultivated, are noble and emancipating; they lead the one who practices them to the complete destruction of suffering.
Thus [ends] the third [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 51.4. (SN 51.4, PTS SN v 255)
1. Cāpāla Chapter:

The Discourse on Disenchantment “Bhikkhus, these four bases for spiritual power, when developed and cultivated, lead to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.”
Which four?

Here, monks, a monk develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of desire and volitional formations of striving; [he develops] the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of energy … [and so on] … peyāla … [concentration of mind … and concentration of investigation].

“He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of mind and volitional formations of striving … [and] the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of investigation and volitional formations of striving.
Monks, these four bases for psychic power, when developed and cultivated, lead to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.”
The Fourth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 51.5 (SN 51.5, PTS SN v 255) 1.
Cāpāla Chapter
The Discourse on the Bases of Psychic Power:
“Bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins in the past have accomplished a portion of psychic power, all did so through having developed and cultivated the four bases of psychic power.
Bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins in the future will accomplish a portion of psychic power, all will do so through having developed and cultivated the four bases of psychic power.”
"Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins at present produce a portion of psychic power, they all do so through the development and cultivation of the four bases of psychic power. Which four?
Here, monks, a monk develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration of desire and volitional formations of striving."

He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of energy and the volitional formations of striving; ... [and so on] ... the concentration of mind; ... [and so on] ... he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of investigation and the volitional formations of striving.
"Whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, in the past have accomplished a portion of psychic power, all did so through having developed and cultivated these very four bases of psychic power.
Whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, in the future will accomplish a portion of psychic power, all will do so through having developed and cultivated these very four bases of psychic power."
“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins at present produce a portion of psychic power, all do so because they have developed and cultivated these very four bases for psychic power.
The fifth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 51.6 (SN 51.6, PTS SN v 256)
1. The Chapter on Cāpāla:

The Discourse on Perfection “Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past have accomplished perfection in psychic power, all of them did so through having developed and cultivated the four bases for psychic power.”
“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will fully accomplish spiritual power, all of them will do so through the development and cultivation of the four bases for spiritual power.
Whatever ascetics or brahmins at present are fully accomplishing spiritual power, all of them do so through the development and cultivation of the four bases for spiritual power. Which four?”

Here, monks, a bhikkhu develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to energy … pe … he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to mind … pe …
He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of investigation and volitional formations of striving.
For whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, have in the past fully accomplished psychic power, all of them did so because they had developed and cultivated these very four bases for psychic power.

And whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, will in the future fully accomplish psychic power, all of them will do so because they will have developed and cultivated these very four bases for psychic power.

“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins at present produce spiritual power in its completeness, all of them do so because they have developed and cultivated these very four bases for spiritual power.
The sixth.

The Discourse on the Buddha “Bhikkhus, there are these four bases for spiritual power.”
Which four?

Here, monks, a monk develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of desire and volitional formations of striving; [he develops] the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of energy … [and so on] … peyāla … [concentration of mind … concentration of investigation].

Sutta on Knowledge:

“‘This is the basis for spiritual power endowed with concentration through desire and volitional formations of striving’—regarding these things unheard before, vision arose in me, bhikkhus, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, and light arose.”

“‘Thus, indeed, this basis for spiritual power endowed with concentration through desire and volitional formations of striving is to be developed,’ monks—regarding these things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.
‘It has been developed,’ monks—regarding these things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.”

The Sutta on the Shrine.
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Then, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One entered Vesālī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Vesālī and returned from his almsround after the meal, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Take your sitting mat, Ānanda;
we shall go to the Cāpāla Shrine for the day’s rest.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and taking his sitting mat, he followed closely behind the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One approached the Cāpāla Shrine; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat.
The Venerable Ānanda, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Ānanda was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Delightful, Ānanda, is Vesālī; delightful is the Udena Shrine, delightful is the Gotamaka Shrine,
delightful is the Sattamba Shrine, delightful is the Bahuputta Shrine, delightful is the Sārandada Shrine,
and delightful is the Cāpāla Shrine.”

“Ānanda, whoever has developed and cultivated the four bases for psychic power—having made them a vehicle, made them a foundation, established them, consolidated them, and properly undertaken them—could, if he so desired, remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.

Now, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has developed and cultivated the four bases for psychic power—having made them a vehicle, made them a foundation, established them, consolidated them, and properly undertaken them.
Therefore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could, if he so desired, remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.”
In this way, although the Blessed One gave such a broad hint and provided such a broad indication, the Venerable Ānanda was unable to penetrate it;
he did not entreat the Blessed One, saying:

"Venerable sir, may the Blessed One remain for an eon! May the Sugata remain for an eon, for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans"—just as his mind was possessed by Māra.
A second time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

“Delightful, Ānanda, is Vesālī; delightful is the Udena Shrine; delightful is the Gotamaka Shrine. A third time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Delightful, Ānanda, is Vesālī; delightful is the Udena Shrine; delightful is the Gotamaka Shrine.”
The Sattamba Cetiya is delightful; the Bahuputta Cetiya is delightful; the Sārandada Cetiya is delightful;
the Cāpāla Cetiya is delightful.

Ānanda, whoever has developed, cultivated, mastered, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken the four bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) could, if he so desired, remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.
“Ānanda, the four bases for spiritual power have been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well-undertaken by the Tathāgata.
If he so desired, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could remain for an eon, or for the remainder of an eon.
Yet even when such a gross sign was being made and such a gross indication was being given, the Venerable Ānanda was unable to penetrate it.
He did not entreat the Blessed One, saying:

"Venerable sir, let the Blessed One remain for an eon; let the Sugata remain for an eon for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans"—just as his mind was possessed by Māra.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Go now, Ānanda, at whatever time you deem appropriate.

“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Rising from his seat, he paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and sat down at the foot of a certain tree not far away.
Then, not long after the Venerable Ānanda had departed, Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, let the Blessed One now attain final Nibbāna; let the Sugata now attain final Nibbāna. Now is the time for the Blessed One’s final Nibbāna, Bhante.
For these words were indeed spoken by the Blessed One:”
“Evil One, I will not attain final nibbāna as long as my monks have not become disciples who are proficient,
disciplined, confident, learned, bearers of the Dhamma, practitioners of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, practitioners of the proper way, and followers of the Dhamma; who,
having mastered their own teacher’s instruction, will proclaim it, teach it, lay it down, and establish it.”
‘They will explain, analyze, and clarify [the Dhamma]; having well refuted with reasoned arguments any opposing doctrines that have arisen, they will teach the Dhamma accompanied by miracles.
And indeed, Bhante, there are now bhikkhus who are the Blessed One’s disciples—competent, disciplined, and confident.
They are learned, bearers of the Dhamma, practitioners of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, practitioners of the proper way, and followers of the Dhamma.
Having mastered their own teacher’s tradition, they declare it, teach it, lay it down, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, and make it clear.
Having well refuted the doctrines of others that have arisen by means of the Dhamma, they teach the Dhamma accompanied by miracles of power.
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One now attain final nibbāna; let the Sugata now attain final nibbāna. Venerable sir, the time has now come for the Blessed One’s final nibbāna.
For this word was indeed spoken by the Blessed One:
‘Evil One, I shall not attain final nibbāna as long as my bhikkhunīs have not become disciples who are accomplished...’”
They will be disciplined, confident, learned, bearers of the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing with proper conduct, and living according to the Dhamma;
having mastered their own teacher’s tradition, they will declare it, teach it, lay it out, establish it, open it up, analyze it, and make it clear,
and they will thoroughly refute the doctrines of others that have arisen by means of the Dhamma.
‘Having restrained them, they will teach the Dhamma with its wonders. Now, Bhante,
there are currently bhikkhunīs who are the Blessed One’s disciples—
discerning, disciplined, confident, learned, bearers of the Dhamma, practitioners of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, practitioners of the proper way, and followers of the Dhamma.
Having mastered their own teacher’s tradition, they declare it, teach it, lay it out, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, and make it clear;
having thoroughly refuted the doctrines of others that have arisen by means of reasoned argument, they teach the Dhamma accompanied by miracles.
"Venerable sir, let the Blessed One now attain final Nibbāna; let the Sugata now attain final Nibbāna. Now is the time for the Blessed One’s final Nibbāna, venerable sir."
Moreover, Bhante, this word was spoken by the Blessed One:
“Evil One, I will not attain final nibbāna as long as my male lay followers...
[as long as] my female lay followers have not become disciples who are accomplished, disciplined, confident, learned, and bearers of the Dhamma.”
Practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing with propriety, and living according to the Dhamma, they— having mastered their own teacher’s tradition—
will declare it, teach it, lay it down, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, and make it clear; and having refuted,
with the aid of the Dhamma, the doctrines of others that have arisen, they will do so in a thoroughly well-refuted and authoritative manner.
‘...will teach the Dhamma.
Now, Bhante, there are at present male lay followers ...
and female lay followers who are disciples of the Blessed One—discerning, disciplined, confident, learned, bearers of the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma.”
Practicing with propriety and living in accordance with the Dhamma, having mastered their own teacher’s tradition,
they declare it, teach it, lay it out, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, and make it clear;
having thoroughly refuted the doctrines of others that have arisen by means of the Dhamma, they teach the Dhamma accompanied by miracles.
“May the Blessed One now attain final Nibbāna, venerable sir; may the Sugata now attain final Nibbāna. Now is the time for the Blessed One’s final Nibbāna, venerable sir.
For this word was spoken by the Blessed One:
‘Evil One, I shall not attain final Nibbāna as long as this holy life has not become successful and prosperous, widely spread, popular, and pervasive, well-proclaimed among gods and humans.’”
“Venerable sir, this holy life of the Blessed One has become successful and prosperous, extended, popular, widespread, well-proclaimed among gods and humans.
Now, venerable sir, let the Blessed One attain final Nibbāna; now, venerable sir, let the Sugata attain final Nibbāna. Now is the time for the Blessed One’s final Nibbāna.
When this was said, the Blessed One said this to Māra the Evil One:
“Be unconcerned, Evil One; the Tathāgata’s final Nibbāna will not be long in coming.
At the end of three months from now, the Tathāgata will attain final Nibbāna.
Then, at the Cāpāla Shrine, the Blessed One, mindful and clearly comprehending, relinquished the life-force constituent.
When the Blessed One had relinquished the life-force, there was a great earthquake, terrifying and hair-raising, and celestial drums resounded.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“The measurable and the immeasurable, and their arising...”
The Sage relinquished the formative force of existence;
delighted within and concentrated,
he shattered his own rebirth like a coat of mail.
The tenth.
The first chapter, the Cāpāla Chapter.
Its summary verse:
The unopposed and the opposed,
the noble and the wearying;
the partial and the complete— these, O bhikkhu, [are the paths].
The Buddha, knowledge, and the shrine.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 51.11 (SN 51.11, PTS SN v 263) 2. Pāsādakampanavagga (The Chapter on the Quaking of the Palace)
The Pubba Sutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, before my full enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, it occurred to me:”
‘What now is the cause, what is the condition for the development of the bases of psychic power?
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘Here, a monk develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving.’”
Thus my mental state will be neither too slack nor too strained, neither too constricted internally nor too distracted externally.
And he dwells perceiving what is behind as before and what is before as behind—just as it was before, so it is behind; just as it is behind, so it was before.
"As below, so above; as above, so below;
as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day.
Thus, with a mind that is open and unenveloped, he develops a mind imbued with luminosity."
He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the volitional formations of striving and concentration through energy, thinking:
"Thus my energy will be neither too slack nor too strained; it will be neither constricted internally nor distracted externally.
And he dwells perceiving what is behind and what is ahead."
As it was before, so it is after; as it is after, so it was before.
As it is below, so it is above; as it is above, so it is below.
As it is by day, so it is by night; as it is by night, so it is by day.
Thus, with a mind that is open and unenveloped, he develops a radiant mind.
He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of mind and volitional formations of striving, [thinking]:
"In this way, my mind will be neither too slack nor too strained; it will not be constricted internally nor distracted externally."
And he dwells perceiving what is behind as before and what is before as behind;
as below so above, as above so below.
As by day, so by night; as by night, so by day.
Thus, with a mind that is open and unenveloped, he develops a luminous mind.
He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving.
Thus my investigation will be neither too slack nor too strained; it will be neither constricted internally nor distracted externally.
And I shall dwell perceiving what is behind as before and what is before as behind—just as it was before, so it is behind; just as it is behind, so it was before.
As below, so above; as above, so below;
as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day.
Thus, with a mind that is open and unenveloped, he develops a mind imbued with luminosity.
When, bhikkhu, these four bases for psychic power have been thus developed and cultivated, one experiences various kinds of psychic power:
having been one, one becomes many; having been many, one becomes one; one appears and disappears;
one passes through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains without being obstructed, as if through space; and one walks upon the earth...
He dives in and out of the earth as if it were water; he walks on water without breaking the surface as if on solid ground;
he travels through the air cross-legged like a winged bird;
with his hand he touches and strokes the sun and moon, so powerful and majestic; and even as far as the Brahma-world, he exercises mastery with his body.

When, bhikkhu, these four bases for psychic power have been thus developed and cultivated, one hears both kinds of sounds with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans—the sounds of gods and of men, whether far or near.
When, bhikkhu, these four bases for psychic power have been thus developed and cultivated, one understands the minds of other beings and other persons by encompassing them with one’s own mind.
One understands a mind affected by lust as “a mind affected by lust”; ... [and so on].
He understands a mind free from lust as ‘a mind free from lust’;
he understands a mind with hatred as ‘a mind with hatred’;
he understands a mind free from hatred as ‘a mind free from hatred’.
He understands a mind with delusion as "a mind with delusion";
he understands a mind free from delusion as "a mind free from delusion";
he understands a contracted mind as "a contracted mind."
He understands a distracted mind as “a distracted mind”;
he understands an exalted mind as “an exalted mind”;
he understands an unexalted mind as “an unexalted mind.”
He understands a surpassed mind as “a surpassed mind”;
he understands an unsurpassed mind as “an unsurpassed mind”;
he understands a concentrated mind as “a concentrated mind.”
He understands an unconcentrated mind as ‘an unconcentrated mind’;
he understands a liberated mind as ‘a liberated mind’;
and he understands an unliberated mind as ‘an unliberated mind.’
When, bhikkhu, these four bases for psychic power have been thus developed and cultivated, one recollects manifold past abodes, that is to say:
one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births... [and so on].

He recollects his manifold past lives, even a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, and many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion:
"In that place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere."
"There I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I reappeared here. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details.
When, monk, these four bases of psychic power have been thus developed and cultivated, by means of the divine eye...
With the pure divine eye, surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate;
he understands how beings fare according to their karma:
"Alas, these worthy beings were possessed of misconduct in body, possessed of misconduct in speech, and possessed of misconduct in mind..."
They were revilers of the noble ones, possessed of wrong view, and undertakers of actions based on wrong view;
with the breakup of the body, after death, they were reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But these venerable beings, endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind, were not revilers of the noble ones.
‘They possessed right view and undertook actions based on right view; with the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a happy destination, a heavenly world.

Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.
“Bhikkhu, when the four bases for spiritual power have been thus developed and cultivated in this way, through the destruction of the taints,
one realizes for oneself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, one dwells therein.
Thus was the first [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 51.12 (SN 51.12, PTS SN v 267) 2. Pāsādakampanavagga Mahapphalasutta The Discourse on Great Fruit At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when one has developed and cultivated the four bases for psychic power, made them a vehicle, made them a basis, established them, and maintained them in being, one may expect one of two fruits: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “When the four bases for psychic power Are developed and well-cultivated, One may expect one of these two fruits: Final knowledge in this very life, Or, if there is a residue remaining, The state of non-returning.”
“Bhikkhus, these four bases for spiritual power, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit.
And how, bhikkhus, are the four bases for spiritual power developed and cultivated so that they are of great fruit and great benefit?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the basis for spiritual power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving.”
Thus my mental application will be neither too slack nor too strained; it will be neither constricted internally nor distracted externally.
And I shall dwell perceiving what is behind as what is before, and what is before as what is behind;
as it was before, so it is behind; as it is behind, so it was before.
As below, so above; as above, so below;
as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day.
Thus, with a mind that is open and unenveloped, he develops a luminous mind.

He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of energy and the volitional formations of striving; ... pe ... he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of mind and the volitional formations of striving; ... he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of investigation and the volitional formations of striving.
Thus my investigation will be neither too slack nor too strained; it will be neither constricted internally nor distracted externally.
And I shall dwell perceiving what is behind as what is before, and what is before as what is behind.
As below, so above; as above, so below;
as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day.
Thus, with a mind that is open and unenveloped, he develops a mind imbued with luminosity.
“Monks, when the four bases for psychic power are thus developed and thus cultivated, they are of great fruit and great benefit.
When the four bases for psychic power have been thus developed and thus cultivated by a monk, he experiences various kinds of psychic power:
having been one, he becomes many … [as before] … he exercises mastery with the body as far as the Brahma world … [as before].”
“Monks, when these four bases for spiritual power have been thus developed and thus cultivated, a bhikkhu, through the destruction of the taints,
enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized them for himself with direct knowledge in this very life.”
The Second.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 51.13 (SN 51.13, PTS SN v 268) 2.
The Chapter on the Quaking of the Palace.
The Discourse on Concentration through Zeal:
“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu, relying on zeal, attains concentration, attains one-pointedness of mind—
this is called concentration through zeal.”
Thus, he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states.
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states.
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states.

He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen.
These are called "volitional formations of striving.
Thus, this desire, this concentration through desire, and these volitional formations of striving—
This, monks, is called the basis for spiritual power endowed with the volitional formation of striving and concentration through desire.
If, monks, a monk, relying on energy, attains concentration, attains one-pointedness of mind—
this is called “concentration through energy.”
Thus, for the sake of the non-arising of unarisen wholesome states,

and for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states, one generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives.
These are called "volitional formations of striving."
Thus, monks, this energy, this concentration of energy, and these volitional formations of striving—
this is called the basis for spiritual power endowed with concentration of energy and volitional formations of striving.
If, monks, a bhikkhu, relying on the mind, attains concentration, attains one-pointedness of mind—
This is called “concentration of mind.
For the non-arising of unwholesome states that have not yet arisen...

[and so on] ...for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have already arisen, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives.
These are called "volitional formations of striving.
Thus, this mind, this concentration of mind, and these volitional formations of striving— this, monks,
is called the basis for spiritual power endowed with concentration of mind and volitional formations of striving.
If, monks, a bhikkhu, relying on investigation, attains concentration, attains one-pointedness of mind—this is called “concentration through investigation.
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states... [as before]...

He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen.
These are called "the formations of striving.
Thus, this is inquiry, this is concentration through inquiry, and these are the formations of striving.
“This, monks, is called the basis for spiritual power endowed with the volitional formations of striving and concentration through investigation. Thus it was said.
The third [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 51.14 (SN 51.14, PTS SN v 269).
2. The Chapter on the Quaking of the Palace;
The Discourse to Moggallāna.
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.

Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were dwelling below in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother—restless, arrogant, fickle, talkative, with loose speech, muddled mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with wandering minds, and with unrestrained senses.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:

“Moggallāna, these fellow celibates are staying here in the Migāramātupāsāda; they are restless, arrogant, fickle, talkative, loose-tongued, muddled in mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with wandering minds and uncontrolled faculties.
Go, Moggallāna, and stir up a sense of spiritual urgency in those bhikkhus.
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied to the Blessed One. Then he performed such a feat of supernormal power...
He performed such a feat that with his big toe he made Migāra’s Mother’s Palace shake, tremble, and quiver.
Then those bhikkhus, stirred with awe and their hair standing on end, stood to one side, saying:
"It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir!"
“Indeed, both the Nivāpa wind and this Palace of Migāra’s Mother have deep foundations, are firmly planted, immovable, and unshakable; yet it has been shaken, trembled, and quaked!
Then the Blessed One approached those bhikkhus; having approached, the Blessed One said to those bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, why are you standing to one side, agitated and with hair standing on end?”
“It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!
This Palace of Migāra’s Mother is indeed sheltered from the wind, with its deep foundations well-planted, immovable and unshakable; yet it has been made to tremble, shake, and quiver!
“Bhikkhus, it was precisely because he wished to stir you to spiritual urgency that the bhikkhu Moggallāna caused the Palace of Migāra’s Mother to tremble, shake, and quiver with his big toe.”
“What do you think, bhikkhus, by having developed and cultivated what things has the bhikkhu Moggallāna become so powerful and so majestic?
“Venerable sir, our teachings have the Blessed One as their root, the Blessed One as their guide, and the Blessed One as their resort. It would be well indeed...”
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One himself explain the meaning of this statement; having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“Therefore, bhikkhus, listen.
It is because of the development and cultivation of the four bases for psychic power that the bhikkhu Moggallāna has become so powerful and so majestic.”
Of which four?

Here, monks, the bhikkhu Moggallāna develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving; [he develops] the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to energy … [and so on].
He develops the basis for spiritual power consisting in concentration of mind accompanied by the volitional formations of striving,
thinking: "Thus my investigation will be neither too slack nor too tense."
It will not be contracted internally, nor will it be distracted externally.
And one dwells perceiving continuity:
as it was before, so it is after; as it is after, so it was before.
As below, so above; as above, so below;
as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day.
Thus, with a mind that is open and unenveloped, he develops a luminous mind.
“Monks, it is because these four bases for spiritual power have been developed and cultivated that the monk Moggallāna has become so powerful and so majestic. And furthermore, monks,

because these four bases for spiritual power have been developed and cultivated, the monk Moggallāna experiences various kinds of supernormal powers … [as before] … he exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma world … And furthermore,
monks, because these four bases for spiritual power have been developed and cultivated, Moggallāna…”
“With the destruction of the taints, a bhikkhu dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom,
and having entered upon it, he abides therein. This is the fourth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 51.15 (SN 51.15, PTS SN v 271) 2. Pāsādakampanavagga Uṇṇābha Brāhmaṇa Sutta At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the brahmin Uṇṇābha approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite conversation and greetings, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, how many kinds of brahmins are there? “There are four kinds of brahmins, brahmin,” the Blessed One replied. “Which four? The one who is a brahmin by birth and lineage, but not by conduct; the one who is a brahmin by conduct, but not by birth; the one who is neither a brahmin by birth nor by conduct; and the one who is a brahmin both by birth and by conduct. And how, brahmin, is one a brahmin by birth and lineage, but not by conduct? Here, brahmin, someone is born of brahmin parents, well-born on both sides, of pure descent for seven generations back, unmarred, untainted, and of irreproachable birth. But he does not practice the conduct of a brahmin. This is called a brahmin by birth and lineage, but not by conduct. And how, brahmin, is one a brahmin by conduct, but not by birth? Here, brahmin, someone is born of non-brahmin parents, not well-born on both sides, not of pure descent for seven generations back, marred, tainted, and of reproachable birth. But he practices the conduct of a brahmin. This is called a brahmin by conduct, but not by birth. And how, brahmin, is one neither a brahmin by birth nor by conduct? Here, brahmin, someone is born of non-brahmin parents... of reproachable birth, and he does not practice the conduct of a brahmin. This is called one who is neither a brahmin by birth nor by conduct. And how, brahmin, is one a brahmin both by birth and by conduct? Here, brahmin, someone is born of brahmin parents, well-born on both sides, of pure descent for seven generations back, unmarred, untainted, and of irreproachable birth; and he also practices the conduct of a brahmin. This is called a brahmin both by birth and by conduct. These, brahmin, are the four kinds of brahmins. When this was said, the brahmin Uṇṇābha said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!
